fiches.name: SMSG_GODMODE
fiches.summary: AzerothCore defines 0x0023 as SMSG_GODMODE and declares it STATUS_NEVER -- the core never sends it -- and Ascension's client keeps the same inherited name in its opcode table. A third-party capture of a live Ascension session reports the realm using the number for something else entirely: three length-prefixed string lists, 79 entries in all, that read as an anti-cheat detector signature set (process and module names, short file tokens, window-title fragments). The name in the table therefore says nothing about the content. Our own contribution is negative and re-derivable: none of the reported signature strings exists in the stock client binaries, so a list like this cannot be compiled in and has to arrive at runtime, which is consistent with a packet carrying it. That does not prove the packet is this one. The client's own anti-cheat reports go back the other way on CMSG_ANTICHEAT_ALERT (0x051f) and CMSG_ANTICHEAT_VERSION (0x0520).

fiches.name: CMSG_TRANSMOG_SPEC_SET_UPDATE
fiches.summary: Named CMSG_TRANSMOG_SPEC_SET_UPDATE by the client's own opcode table, the last member of the legacy 0x0540-0x0559 range. Unlike its neighbours this opcode does have one raw byte match for a `mov esi, 0x559` encoding in Extensions.dll's `.text` (RVA 0x4e1010), but it is not real code: Ghidra's own analysis at that address reports "Control flow encountered bad instruction data" and halts, meaning the disassembly before and after it does not resolve to valid instructions either -- the match is a coincidental five-byte pattern inside non-code bytes, not a sender. No walkable `push 0x559` -> `Put(u32)` -> `Send` sequence exists there or anywhere else in the section. The capture reference does not name a specific modern-cluster opcode that replaces this one (unlike the rest of the legacy suite, which it maps to named successors); it only places 0x0559 inside the same superseded numeric range as a whole. What "spec" refers to here -- talent spec, a per-loadout appearance set, or something else -- is not established by anything read in this pass.

fiches.name: SMSG_CHALLENGE_CREATOR_QUERY_CHALLENGES_RESULT
fiches.summary: The custom-trial list for the challenge creator. A clear flag, a fire flag, a count, then one trial record each: id, an owned byte, four more strings this fiche does not identify, a list of (challengeId, level, description) entries, the viewer's two vote bytes and two lists of (guid, 0) vote records. TRIAL_QUERY_RESULT fires at the end when the second byte is set. The DISAGREEMENT recorded against this opcode is RESOLVED: the fork's SendTrialData writes exactly this shape, field for field. The 2026-09-19 check saw fewer server fields because server_layout.py skips an AppendConfigString whose argument is a call expression (the three middle strings) and does not follow AppendVoteList (the two vote lists), and because it concatenated both branches of the empty-result if.

layout.name: trialId
layout.notes: u32 length then that many bytes, no NUL (FUN_100d3680). The whole handler is this one read: it fetches the trial manager (FUN_10124310) and assigns the string into the manager at +0xc, guarded by the usual std::string self-assignment test, then frees the temporary and returns. Nothing else is read and no event is fired. The fork's SendActiveTrial writes exactly one AppendConfigString(trialID), so the two sides agree; an empty string clears the client's active trial.

fiches.name: SMSG_CHALLENGE_CREATOR_ACTIVE_CHALLENGE_UPDATE
fiches.summary: The player's active custom trial: one length-prefixed trial id, assigned into the trial manager at +0xc (empty clears it). The DISAGREEMENT recorded against this opcode is RESOLVED, and both halves of it were run-on artefacts of the same pair of functions. Server side: server_layout.py's chain ran out of SendActiveTrial (one string) into the next function in the file, AppendTrialCompletionEntry, whose nine fields belong to the trial-completion packet -- hence the phantom 'ten fields'. Client side: Ghidra's decompilation of FUN_101226d0 runs past a noreturn __fastfail (swi(0x29)) in the string destructor's bounds check and continues into the next function, FUN_10122780, which handlers.yaml registers for 0x05CB SMSG_CHALLENGE_CREATOR_COMPLETION -- that function, not this one, installs a second SEH frame, parses 0x88-byte completion records through FUN_10125860 and fires TRIAL_COMPLETION_ADDED with %s%u.

fiches.name: SMSG_CHALLENGE_QUERY_COMPLETION_RESPONSE
fiches.summary: The trial leaderboard: a challengeID, a level, a count and that many completion records. Each record independently repeats the challengeID and level, then a player name, a start time and a complete time (each padded to 8 bytes, high dword always zero) and three more strings (race, gender, class), all four strings length-prefixed with no NUL. Read from the handler at 0x001376b0, its record parser at 0x0013efd0 and, for record field names, the Lua-table converter at 0x0013bf30 (all decompiled, DecompAt.java; the handler and parser 2026-09-20 under GHIDRA_WORKSPACE=unclassified, the converter re-decompiled and its callers checked 2026-09-20 under GHIDRA_WORKSPACE=verify-unclassified). Skeptic correction: the converter is not called by the packet handler's per-record loop -- `Callers.java` finds exactly one caller of 0x0013bf30, `FUN_10140ab0`, a distinct function with no reference anywhere in the SMSG 0x05C7 handler or its parser. The loop instead calls a generic, 86-caller helper (`FUN_1013b8b0`) after each parse. What the loop actually builds is a 0x78-byte-strided C++ struct vector; `FUN_10140ab0` walks that same stride over a vector and calls the converter on each element -- almost certainly a Lua-facing getter invoked later, on demand, not during packet receipt. The record field *names* still stand, because the offsets the converter reads (0, 1, 2-7, 8, 10, 0xc-0x11, 0x12-0x17, 0x18-0x1d) line up exactly with the offsets the parser writes -- re-verified independently below -- but the claim that the handler calls the converter per record does not survive and is corrected.

layout.name: challengeId
layout.notes: record +0x00. The handler builds the completion store's key from record dwords 0 and 1 (FUN_10130150 then FUN_101305b0) and appends the 0x78 entry to the bucket it finds; the Lua getter over that store is C_Challenge.GetChallengeCompletions(challengeID, level, count) (ChallengeExtendedInfoMixin.lua:199, L2), so the PAIR is the (challengeID, level) key -- that much is read. Which of the two is which follows the getter's argument order and the fork's writer, and is not itself read out. The same two dwords are the first two %u of CHALLENGE_COMPLETION_ADDED; its third is the new entry's index, not a packet field.

layout.name: level
layout.notes: record +0x04; the other half of the store key (see above)

layout.name: playerName
layout.notes: u32 length then bytes, no NUL (FUN_100d3680), move-assigned into record +0x08; a std::string is 0x18 here, so it spans +0x08..+0x1f. Named: it is the only string before the two time pairs, and the leaderboard model's only such key is PlayerName (ChallengeExtendedInfoMixin.lua:230-268, L2).

layout.name: startTime
layout.notes: record +0x20. Read with the next dword in one 8-byte cursor bump -- the client's 64-bit lo/hi idiom -- so the two pairs are two 64-bit times. The UI computes CompleteTime - StartTime as a duration and formats CompleteTime with date() (L2); which pair is the start follows the fork's writer and the fact that a completion cannot precede its start.

layout.name: startTimeHigh
layout.notes: record +0x24; the high half. The fork sends 0.

layout.name: completeTime
layout.notes: record +0x28; the second pair, one 8-byte cursor bump

layout.name: completeTimeHigh
layout.notes: record +0x2c. The fork sends 0.

layout.name: playerRace
layout.notes: record +0x30. Three length-prefixed strings close the record; the parser names none of them and the converter that builds the Lua table is not decompiled here. The leaderboard model's remaining keys are PlayerRace, PlayerGender and PlayerClass (L2) -- the SET is forced, the ORDER within it is the fork's (L1). The UI slices them with :sub(6), :sub(8) and GetLeaderboardClassInfo, i.e. RACE_*, GENDER_* and CLASS_* tokens.

layout.name: playerGender
layout.notes: record +0x48

layout.name: playerClass
layout.notes: record +0x60; ends at +0x78, exactly the 0x78 stride the handler advances the completion vector by, so the record map closes.

fiches.name: SMSG_CHALLENGE_COMPLETION
fiches.summary: One leaderboard completion entry, inserted into the completion store and followed by CHALLENGE_COMPLETION_ADDED. Ten fields, read by the parser FUN_1013efd0: two u32, a length-prefixed name, two 64-bit times each read as a lo/hi pair, and three length-prefixed tokens. The record ends at +0x78 -- exactly the stride the handler advances by, so the map is complete. The first two dwords are the store key the Lua getter takes as (challengeID, level); the names of the three trailing strings come from the leaderboard model, whose key set forces them but whose order is the fork's.

fiches.name: CMSG_TRANSMOG_COMPONENT_APPLY
fiches.summary: Named CMSG_TRANSMOG_COMPONENT_APPLY by the client's own opcode table, with its own small SMSG pair immediately after it in the table (0x05ce SMSG_TRANSMOG_COMPONENT_UPDATE, 0x05d1 SMSG_TRANSMOG_COMPONENT_SUCCESS -- see those fiches; 0x05cf/0x05d0 sit unnamed between them). Nothing in this build constructs a packet with this opcode: no `push 0x5cd` / `mov r32, 0x5cd` occurs anywhere in Extensions.dll's `.text`, byte-exhaustively. The capture reference groups it with the rest of the legacy suite as superseded but does not name a specific modern-cluster opcode that replaces the "component" concept the way it does for outfits or the visibility toggle; what a "transmog component" was (a sub-slot of an appearance? an ingredient item?) is not established by anything read in this pass.

fiches.name: SMSG_TRANSMOG_COMPONENT_UPDATE
fiches.summary: Named SMSG_TRANSMOG_COMPONENT_UPDATE by the client's own opcode table, sitting right after CMSG_TRANSMOG_COMPONENT_APPLY (0x05cd) and before SMSG_TRANSMOG_COMPONENT_SUCCESS (0x05d1, with two unnamed opcodes 0x05cf/0x05d0 between them) -- the natural reading is a server push of a changed component followed by a success ack for the apply, but nothing in this build has code to send either half of that: the client registers no handler for 0x05ce. The registration scan (`handlers.yaml`) is exhaustive over every static `push handler; push opcode; call <registrar>` site across all three registrars Extensions.dll uses (532 total registrations, including the far-higher 0x09bf in an unrelated family -- see that fiche), so the usual "Extensions.dll-only" caveat for a *standard* opcode (client/symbols/.../handlers.md) does not apply here: 0x05ce is outside AzerothCore's baseline entirely (protocol/known-baseline.yaml), so stock Ascension.exe code has no notion of it either -- there is nowhere else a handler could live.

fiches.name: SMSG_PATCH_CHR_SPECS
fiches.summary: One row of ChrSpecs.dbc: 33 dwords (132 bytes), of which 15 are throwaway placeholders overwritten by 15 trailing lpstrings the wire sends right after, in an order this pass confirmed from the handler's own stack layout. All 33 dwords are named from the client's native getter C_ClassInfo.GetSpecInfo (VA 0x100dac60, called from GameTooltip.lua:259-260), which builds a Lua table from exactly this set of offsets -- 18 scalar/boolean columns plus 4 three-element lists (PrimaryStats, PrimaryResources, SecondaryResources, ExampleSpells) this pass numbered itself, since the getter names each list once, not element by element. fiches.summary: SMSG_PATCH_LOADING_SCREENS: despite the name, this handler does not touch any of the 114 CustomDBCMgr table objects -- no minId/maxId/rows-array reference anywhere in the decompiled C. It looks its key up in a hash-map-style container (FUN_100b1bd0) and inserts through a matching helper (FUN_100ab220), the pattern patch-tables.md calls out for the other 141 patch handlers that store into a DLL-internal container rather than a client DBC row. The opcode's own name happens to match LoadingScreens.dbc, a real 4-field/16-byte table in the snapshot, but nothing here ties the two together -- that binding (patch-table-names.md's 'L0 name' bucket) is exactly this: an inferred label from the opcode's own text, not a confirmed table write. fiches.summary: One row of SkillCard.dbc: 12 dwords (48 bytes), of which the 4 at +0x14..+0x20 arrive as throwaway placeholders and are then overwritten by 4 length-prefixed strings the wire sends right after. All 12 fields are named from the client's own Lua-table builder for this row, FUN_1009bc60 (VA 0x1009bc60, client/symbols/.../lua-keys.yaml's f_1009bc60), which pushes each one by an explicit key literal read at the matching record offset; two of its key literals (Rank at +0x08, Type at +0x14) are .rdata strings the automatic extractor did not capture. lua-keys.yaml's own offset for CollectedRank (16) is a false pairing: FUN_1009bc60 shows CollectedRank is computed from a separate per-player hashmap, not read from the record, so that key is not one of this row's columns.

fiches.name: SMSG_OPEN_COLLECTOR_CACHE_RESULT
fiches.summary: Named SMSG_OPEN_COLLECTOR_CACHE_RESULT by the client's own opcode table, the very next slot after CMSG_OPEN_COLLECTOR_CACHE (0x06df -- not ours, but very much alive: the Lua binding `OpenCollectorCache` at RVA 0x00194830 constructs a `CDataStore`, writes opcode 0x6df, `PutData`s one caller-supplied `u32`, `Finalize`s and sends -- read directly from its decompilation in this pass). The natural reading is that 0x06e0 is that request's server-to-client answer, and the "Collector Cache" feature itself is real and patched into this client (four DBC tables -- `CollectorCacheTypes`/`RarityTypes`/`RarityRates`/ `Items` -- loaded via the SMSG_PATCH_* stream at 0x06d9-0x06dc, plus Lua getters `GetCollectorCacheItemInfo`/`GetCollectorCacheItems`/`GetCollectorCacheRarityRatesInfo`/ `GetCollectorCacheRarityTypeInfo`/`GetCollectorCacheTypeInfo`/`GetNumCollectorCacheItems`). But this specific opcode, the result, has no handler registered in this build: whatever the request opens, the client does not read a reply on 0x06e0 to learn about it. Either the result already lives in the patched DBC data the getters above read (so "opening" the cache needs no live reply), or it arrives some other way this pass did not trace (an item delivery, a UI refresh triggered off something else).

layout.name: result
layout.notes: A CA_INSPECT_* token, matched in source order against a table of six strings starting at CA_INSPECT_OK (PTR_s_CA_INSPECT_OK_10b34640). The handler fires INSPECT_CHARACTER_ADVANCEMENT_RESULT(result). Only index 0, CA_INSPECT_OK, reads further: on every other token nothing after the string is touched, so a failure is the string alone. An unmatched token falls through to the handler's "Unexpected Value: {}" path, which also reads nothing more.

layout.name: targetGuid
layout.notes: CA_INSPECT_OK only. Read as two u32 -- low at payload +0x00 of the body, high at +0x04 -- and recombined as CONCAT44(high, low). The pair keys the inspect-target lookup FUN_1016f700 and the recombined value is compared against the local player's GUID at the end of the handler before it refreshes the frame.

layout.name: activeSlot
layout.notes: CA_INSPECT_OK only, body +0x08. Passed to FUN_101499e0 -- the same setter that 0x0725's first field feeds, which that fiche proves at L5 to be the zero-based active specialization slot. Here it is the inspected character's.

layout.name: slotCount
layout.notes: CA_INSPECT_OK only, body +0x0c. The loop bound: the handler iterates index 0..slotCount-1, fetching each slot container with FUN_10149480(index) and creating it with FUN_10149380(index) when absent, and reads one known-entries block per iteration. 0x0725's second field (slotCount) feeds the twin setter FUN_101499f0. If a container can be neither fetched nor created the handler abandons the packet.

fields.name: count
fields.notes: One complete known-entries block per slot, read by FUN_10166760 (RVA 0x00166760) -- literally the same call 0x0726's handler makes at 0x001713c4, with the same packet cursor. The block is a u32 count followed by that many 21-byte records, and the result is stored into the slot with FUN_10158010, again as in 0x0726.

fields.name: reserved

What each field MEANS, and how each is graded, belongs to 0x0726: there entryId and flag are L5, rank L3, and marker, buildTime and reserved L1. Nothing here raises them.

Despite sharing decompiled code with 0x0691 (Ghidra put both opcodes' handlers in one function at 0x101dca00), this opcode's own entry point (registration RVA 0x001e6b4b, reached via the label at 0x101dcd30) only ever touches AppearanceDetails.dbc's row array (0x10bdfa4c matches its CustomDBCMgr object exactly) -- AppearanceCategories.dbc, which patch-tables.yaml also lists for this opcode, is written by 0x0691's own entry point, not this one. fiches.name: SMSG_UNNAMED_0725

layout.name: count
layout.notes: The packet carries the COMPLETE set and replaces the client's container. Proven: count=0 clears it and IsKnownID goes false for an entry that was known a moment before. The capture reference reports a login burst of twelve 0x0726 in one session, the first eleven with count = 1..11 and then a full eleven-record set in a different order, for payload sizes of 25 to 235 bytes. 4 + 21*1 = 25 and 4 + 21*11 = 235 exactly, so their sizes confirm this count and the 21-byte record below with nothing trailing it. A growing series is not a delta protocol: each packet is complete as of its moment, which is what this field means.

fields.name: entryId
fields.notes: CharacterAdvancement.dbc entry id. PRESENCE IN THE SET is what makes IsKnownID(entryId) answer true -- no other field is required.

fields.name: rank
fields.notes: THE RANK, by shape. Decompiled: the advancement service's rank getter (RVA 0x00152920) walks a vector with stride 0x20, matches the key at record +0x04 and returns record +0x08 -- exactly where this field lands. An earlier note here said the opposite, reasoning from #4128's unverified claim that the rank is read at +0x14; the normal path never reads +0x14. The lab's 0 is explained and is NOT a packet problem: three accessors read one vector keyed at +0x04 -- membership, this rank at +0x08, and the lock byte at +0x10. IsLockedID matched the raw entry id in the very same forged record, so the record is stored and keyed correctly. GetTalentRankByID is the only accessor RESOLVED. The rank is stored here correctly; the client cannot read it back. GetTalentRankByID first consults the WILDCARD store (0x2c records, filled by SMSG_WILDCARD_ENTRY_LEARNED 0x0621), which is empty outside that game mode, then falls back to this store keyed on *(catalogue_entry + 0) -- not the entry id, so it never matches. Proven by one forged record: u8=1 made IsLockedID true, which requires +0x04 == 31194 in this very vector, while +0x08=5 still read back as 0. A client defect, not a packet or server one. See client/symbols/.../rank-source.md. The capture reference reports rank = 1 in every record of its sample, which is consistent but proves nothing about which offset the client reads back.

fields.name: marker
fields.notes: Third-party claim (#4128): 2 on automatic/implicit nodes, 1 elsewhere. Shipped as 0 by #4027. Sent as 0, 1 and 2 with no observable effect on IsKnownID, IsLockedID, IsTalentID or GetTalentRankByID. Whatever it selects, it is not any of those. The capture reference reports this u32 as the constant 1 in every record of a real login burst. That is COMPATIBLE with the lab, not a contradiction: the lab showed only that 0, 1 and 2 leave those four predicates unchanged, which says nothing about what a live server chose to send. Taken together the two readings say a real server sends 1 for ordinary entries, #4128 says 2 for automatic ones, and no client predicate we have queried can tell the difference. The consumer that distinguishes them has still not been found -- that is the open question, and it is unchanged.

fields.name: flag
fields.notes: THIS IS A LOCK FLAG, NOT A KNOWN GATE. Proven on a real client: 0 leaves the entry unlocked, and 1, 2 and 255 all make IsLockedID(entry) answer true, while IsKnownID stays true in every case. #4128's reading -- that IsKnownID requires this byte to be 1 -- does not hold here. A locked entry is one the UI refuses to interact with, which looks like "the entry did not work" without being the same thing; that is very likely what was observed in game. The capture reference, by the same author as #4128, reports this byte as the constant 0 in every record of a live capture. A live server therefore sent 0 on entries the client plainly treated as known, which is what the lab proves and the opposite of what #4128 concluded. #4128's gate reading should be considered withdrawn by its own author's capture.

fields.name: buildTime
fields.notes: Name from #4128. Shipped as 0 by #4027, and forging it has never been tested. The capture reference calls it a content/build timestamp and reports the single value 0x6A501487 in every record of its sample. Read as a little-endian u32 Unix timestamp that is 1783633031 = 2026-07-09 21:37:11 UTC; the reference's own parenthetical says 2026-07-06, so their value and their date disagree by three days and we cannot tell which they meant. What survives that discrepancy is the shape: one value, identical across every record of one session, in the plausible range for a 2026 epoch second. That reads like a per-content-build stamp rather than anything per-entry -- but it is their capture, not ours, and no consumer of this field has been found in the binary. Still L1.

fields.name: reserved
fields.notes: Observed 0 in every source, the capture reference included, which reports it as a constant 0 across a live session. Never forged, and no read of it has been found. Its presence, rather than its value, is what the reference's 21-byte record and its 4 + 21n payload sizes confirm: there is a sixth field and nothing after it.

fiches.name: CMSG_MULTIPLE_MOVES_BETTER
fiches.summary: Named CMSG_MULTIPLE_MOVES_BETTER by the client's own opcode table -- not the same opcode as AzerothCore's own SMSG_MULTIPLE_MOVES (0x51E, "uncompressed version of SMSG_COMPRESSED_MOVES", `src/server/game/Server/Protocol/Opcodes.h:1340`), and not a duplicate of it: different number, different direction, and this one is client-to-server. `client/client-senders.md` states plainly that this opcode "is a name with no trace either": not a 32- or 16-bit immediate in `.text`, not a value in `.rdata`/`.data`, not an arithmetic constant before a `Put(u32)` opcode write, and not a number in the shipped Lua. This build has no sender for it; layout is not established because there is nothing to read, not because nobody has looked. The three files this fiche used to cite under `used_by_server` were checked by hand and are false positives of a bare-literal scan: `0x0800` in each is an unrelated bitmask (`GameModeDef`'s `BuildDraft` bit and `REGEN_CAST_RANGE`), never an opcode. See the retraction in provenance.

fiches.name: SMSG_MULTIPLE_MOVES_BETTER

Not among the 532 handlers the exhaustive push/push/call registrar scan of `.text` finds (`tools/extract/opcode_handlers.py`, three registrars, `client/symbols/ascension-extensions-2026-08-13/handlers.yaml`); this build registers no handler for it, and the server modules in this fork never send it either (`client/server-usage.yaml` has no entry for it, not even a false-positive literal). Layout is not established because there is nothing to read, not because nobody has looked.

fiches.name: SMSG_PATCH_SPELL
fiches.summary: Named SMSG_PATCH_SPELL by the client's own opcode table. One row of the stock Spell.dbc (AzerothCore already loads this table; ADR 0005), sent as an opaque 680-byte blob (RVA 0x00231de0, no per-field split available) followed by 4 lpstrings. Spell.dbc's own file has exactly 4 locale-string blocks (SpellName, Rank, Description, ToolTip -- the last two fully commented out of SpellEntry) and 234 columns total; the numeric arithmetic closes exactly (234 - 4x16 string slots = 170 dwords = 680 bytes, matching the blob), which is a stronger reconciliation than most opcodes in this bucket get. Even so, this fiche does not decompose the 680-byte blob into named columns or the 4 lpstrings into SpellName/Rank/Description/ToolTip: the blob is a single un-individuated read, so nothing establishes that the internal byte order was not reshuffled during packing even though the total closes, and a sibling table (SkillLine, 0x0933) that looks structurally identical has a string-block count that does NOT reconcile with its lpstring count (3 vs 4), which is direct evidence that this project's assumption "one lpstring per locale block, in file order" fails at least once and should not be trusted anywhere it is not independently confirmed. DBCStructure.h (SpellEntry) and DBCfmt.h (SpellEntryfmt) were checked; no naming source safe enough to assert per-field was found. Read against the real decompiled handler (build/ghidra/handlers-c/0x092a.c): confirms the blob is one 170-dword (0xaa) copy loop and the 4 strings are 4 separate, sequential FUN_100d3680 calls in a fixed order -- consistent with, and no stronger than, the structure already in this layout. The same function also inspects and conditionally rewrites 3 pairs of fields after the copy (comparing one member of each pair against 0x6b/0x6c and the other against 30), a plausible fit for 3 of SpellEntry's MAX_SPELL_EFFECTS arrays, but Ghidra's declared locals for that logic do not reliably map to fixed byte offsets inside the 680-byte blob (the copy loop's destination array is declared shorter than the copy itself and spills into adjacent locals in a way this pass could not safely resolve to specific columns), so nothing further is asserted from it.

fiches.name: SMSG_PATCH_SPELL_VISUAL
fiches.summary: One row of the stock SpellVisual.dbc (AzerothCore already loads this table; ADR 0005), sent as the single 128-byte blob the handler at RVA 0x002331f0 reads (L3, no per-field split available). Nothing was elided (32 cols x 4 bytes = 128 bytes matches the client header exactly), so the blob is decomposed here one dword per column in file order. Only 3 of 32 are named: HasMissile and MissileModel are SpellVisualEntry's only active members; Id is FT_SORT ('d') and commented out of the struct but DBCStructure.h still labels it. The other 29 are core 'x' columns with no name anywhere in AzerothCore (L1 for the 3 names and for the column boundaries themselves, since only the total width was independently decompiled).

fiches.name: SMSG_PATCH_SPELL_VISUAL_KIT_MODEL_ATTACH
fiches.summary: Named SMSG_PATCH_SPELL_VISUAL_KIT_MODEL_ATTACH by the client's own opcode table. It is not read from the wire (the read-position advance stops at 0x14 = 5 dwords) and is therefore not listed as a layout field, but the earlier draft of this fiche did not mention it at all despite claiming to have fully hand-read the decompile; flagged here as an open question, the same way 0x0949's local_38/local_30 are, not silently dropped.

fiches.name: SMSG_REALM_INFO
fiches.summary: Realm parameters the client keeps in one struct (FUN_1008e2d0) and exposes through C_Realm-style getters: realmId at +4, expansion at +8 (GetRealmMaxLevel maps it to 25/35/45/55), a maintenance flag at +0x18 gated by the first u8 flag at +0x40, the auction cut rate at +0x1c. The nine leading fields are the ones azerothcore-wotlk-coa#4128 reproduced; the handler goes on to read eight u8 flags, two NUL-terminated strings, a u8 and a conditional trailing u32 not decoded here. Widths from the asm idiom (floats by movss); names from the getters (L3); the unnamed fields are stored but no getter read here consumes them.

layout.name: eventKey
layout.notes: The low u16 of the block's first dword is the map key: the handler writes it to the node at +0x0e, stores the 52-byte block at node +0x10, and every later lookup compares (ushort)block[0] against that key. The capture reference names it quest_id and reports 147 of its 178 sampled values resolving in Quest.dbc, range 114-2900 (L1).

layout.name: unknown_2
layout.notes: block +0x02..+0x12, copied but never read by this handler. The capture reference decodes +0x02 as a u16 flags word (0x2000, 0xA000, 0x4801, 0x8000, 0x0000, 0xE400) and +0x03 as a u32 unix start time (L1); those two overlap byte +0x03, so its offsets cannot both be right and nothing in this handler settles which -- in its own sample row bytes +0x07..+0x13 are zero. Whether the field at +0x02 is a u16 or a u8 followed by a misaligned u32 is not established.

layout.name: activeFlag
layout.notes: block +0x13 (node +0x23). Non-zero fires GAME_EVENT_STARTED, zero fires GAME_EVENT_ENDED, and in both branches the event fires only when the entry the map already held disagrees; otherwise the handler returns without firing.

layout.name: unknown_4
layout.notes: block +0x14..+0x33, copied but never read by this handler. The capture reference decodes +0x14 as an int32 interval (-60, 60, 2700, 3600, 7200, 9000, 14400, 86400), +0x18 as always zero, +0x1c as a window (0x128A1800 in 162 of 178 rows, else 604800, 10800 or 0x151800), +0x24 as a byte-equal copy of the start time and +0x2c as a unix end time spanning 2026-2031; it does not describe +0x20, +0x28 or +0x30 (L1). It reads the whole packet as a per-quest availability row and leaves the field roles probabilistic.

fiches.name: SMSG_GAME_EVENT_INFO
fiches.summary: One 52-byte block, read as thirteen u32 and stored in a map keyed by the block's first u16; the byte at block +0x13 decides whether GAME_EVENT_STARTED or GAME_EVENT_ENDED fires. The capture reference's packets are 52 bytes too, so the two readings agree on the wire and differ only in how much of the block they decode; its field decode is carried here at L1.

fiches.name: SMSG_SEASONAL_COLLECTION_UNLOCKED
fiches.summary: Seasonal collection unlocked: no packet read is visible in the handler, and none is needed. `handler_0x09bf` takes no field from the `CDataStore` at all; it calls `FUN_10310320()` -- a lazily-constructed singleton whose vftable Ghidra itself names `SeasonalCollectionMgr::vftable` -- and sets the byte at `+0xa0` on it to 1. The mere arrival of the opcode is the whole payload. This reads as a durable one-shot unlock flag, not a report of *what* unlocked: the Lua-exposed getter `IsSeasonalCollectionUnlocked` (bound at the very same address the handler jumps through, RVA 0x003111d0) reads that identical `+0xa0` byte and returns it to Lua as a boolean, so the handler and the getter are provably reading and writing the same field, cross-checked two ways in this build. A companion opcode, 0x09be (handler RVA 0x10310430, not ours), sits right before it and is not examined here.

fiches.name: CMSG_MISSILE_FIRE_POSITION

fiches.name: SMSG_PATCH_CHR_CLASSES_ROLES
fiches.summary: One row of ChrClassesRoles.dbc, written straight into the client's own copy of that table (patch-tables.yaml's CustomDBCMgr scan binds this opcode to it, and the decompile confirms the idiom: the row goes into the table object's rows array at (id - minId), bounds-checked against minId/maxId, exactly as client/patch-tables.md describes). The 11 fields are read off the wire in a flat sequential order (offsets 0x00..0x28) but the client re-orders 5 of them when it stores the row (see field_3/field_4/field_6/field_8/field_9 below) -- the table's own column order is therefore not the wire order. No source in this repository names any of the 11 columns: checked handler-strings.yaml, lua-keys.yaml and the UI corpus (see naming_source below).

layout.name: row
layout.notes: the wire's fixed 16-byte part (cursor advances by exactly 0x10 before the trailing string). Of its four 4-byte columns, the client reads three into named values -- offset 0x00 (the id, used for the minId/maxId bounds check and stored at row slot 0), offset 0x08 (stored at row slot 2) and offset 0x0c (stored at row slot 3) -- and never reads offset 0x04 into a value at all (build/ghidra/handlers-c/0x09d2.c, re-read this pass: `uVar13 = [+8]; uVar4 = [+0]; uVar5 = [+0xc]`, no read of `[+4]`). Row slot 1 (where offset 0x04's raw dword would land) is instead filled with the pointer to field_1 (`puVar9[1] = (uint)pcVar8`) -- offset 0x04 is this table's string-offset column, matching client/patch-tables.md's "the client stitches the row's strings over the record's string-offset fields" note. width: L3 (patches_table.record_size below, and the decompiled reads above). name: none -- no naming source found (see naming_source below).

layout.name: field_1
layout.notes: a NUL-terminated string read right after the 16-byte fixed part (the read cursor advances by 16 + strlen + 1). width/kind: L3 -- re-decompiled this pass (build/ghidra/handlers-c/0x09d2.c: the byte-scan loop `while (*p++ != 0)` and the cursor update `pos = pos_before + 0x11 + (scanned - 1)`, i.e. 16 + string length including the NUL); the earlier stub had this typed `unknown`, which was a placeholder for "computed length", not a claim the kind was unresolved. This is the row's column 2 (offset 0x04, see field_0's note), stitched in from the wire's trailing bytes rather than sent as a raw string-block offset. name: none -- no naming source found.

fiches.name: SMSG_PATCH_OCCLUSION_VOLUME
fiches.summary: One row of OcclusionVolume.dbc, written into the client's own copy of that table (patch-tables.yaml's CustomDBCMgr scan binds this opcode to it, and the decompile confirms the idiom: the row goes into the table object's rows array at (id - minId), bounds-checked against minId/maxId, exactly as client/patch-tables.md describes). The wire's 16-byte fixed part is not a plain 4-dword block copy: the client reads only 3 of its 4 dwords into named values (offsets 0x00, 0x08, 0x0c; the dword at 0x04 is never read into a value at all) and then, at store time, places the trailing cstring's pointer into that 4th row slot instead -- exactly the "string stitched over the record's string-offset column" pattern client/patch-tables.md describes, just with the stitched column in the middle of the row rather than at its end. No source in this repository names any of the table's 4 columns: checked handler-strings.yaml, lua-keys.yaml and the UI corpus (see naming_source below).
